sourcePolicy: Official EU institutions, national sources and quality European tech journalism. Stories without a clear EU or European-country angle are excluded. Retention window is 120 days.

articles.title: Maastricht’s Clementine raises €1.7M to scale its AI hearing-care agent
articles.description: Dutch startup Clementine closed a €1.7 million seed round led by Healthy.Capital to expand Matthew, an AI agent that helps hearing clinics convert inquiries into patients.
articles.content: Founded in Maastricht in 2024, Clementine positions itself as an AI hearing-activation platform. Its agent answers clinic inquiries around the clock, educates prospective patients and guides them into care. The seed funding will deepen the product and expand partnerships with hearing clinics and related healthcare organisations in Europe and North America.

articles.title: Paris-based Hugging Face launches $399 open-source Microduck robot
articles.description: Hugging Face and Bordeaux subsidiary Pollen Robotics unveiled Microduck, a $399 open-source robot that developers can train with reinforcement learning.
articles.content: The 25-centimetre robot can walk, pick up objects with its beak, recover from falls and even roller-skate. It ships with camera, lidar and motion sensors, and its SDK and training stack are open source. Pre-orders topped $2.6 million in the first 24 hours. The product continues Hugging Face’s push from models into physical AI after acquiring Pollen Robotics.

articles.title: German startups raise a record €9.36 billion as capital shifts to AI, robotics and defence
articles.description: PitchBook data reported by Handelsblatt show German startups raised €9.36 billion from January to July 2026, already above the 2022 full-year pace, led by AI, robotics and defence firms.
articles.content: Helsing, Quantum Systems and Stark Defence together raised more than €3 billion earlier in the year, with Neura Robotics adding more than €1 billion in July. Investors expect a new annual record. Unlike the pandemic-era consumer boom, the 2026 surge is concentrated in companies already established in industrial, defence and AI markets.

articles.title: Poland prepares a special law to speed an AI Gigafactory bid of up to €10 billion
articles.description: Warsaw is considering fast-track legislation and has already pledged compute offtake as it competes for a mid-sized EU AI Gigafactory.
articles.content: Poland signed the EuroHPC joint procurement agreement and adopted a resolution guaranteeing access, with an initial national commitment of more than PLN 400 million to buy compute. Public support for a Polish site could reach €1 billion. Officials describe a mid-scale facility of at least 75,000 AI accelerators. Demand from member states already exceeds the seven sites the EU programme envisages.

articles.title: Spain is the only EU bidder putting the state in control of an AI Gigafactory consortium
articles.description: SETT, Spain’s public digital-transformation company, holds 47.99% of the consortium bidding for an EU AI Gigafactory, plus a 1% Catalan government stake.
articles.content: El Economista reports that Germany, France, Italy, Portugal and Poland are backing bids with public money or offtake commitments but have not taken controlling equity. Spain’s structure makes the state the largest shareholder. France has pledged about €100 million as a compute customer rather than an owner. The contrast highlights different national approaches to EU compute sovereignty.

articles.title: UK startup Callosum raises $100 million seed to run AI across mixed chips and models
articles.description: Cambridge-founded Callosum closed a $100 million seed led by Atomico to build software that runs AI workloads across heterogeneous chips and models.
articles.content: Plural, DCVC and the UK Sovereign AI programme also participated. Callosum argues that real-world problems need mixed models and hardware rather than a single model on identical GPUs. The company has partnered with Cerebras and previously raised $10.25 million when it left stealth. The round is one of Europe’s largest AI seed financings of 2026.

articles.title: CEPR analysis: AI Act transparency applies while high-risk rules slip to 2027–28
articles.description: A VoxEU column argues that the Digital Omnibus left Europe in a double bind: Article 50 transparency took effect on 2 August 2026, but standalone high-risk obligations move to December 2027.
articles.content: Regulation 2026/1744 deferred Annex III high-risk rules by 16 months and product-embedded high-risk AI to August 2028. What remains in force is the duty to tell people when they interact with AI and to mark synthetic media. The authors say the delay preserves some competitiveness but weakens the EU’s claim to set the first fully operational high-risk AI regime.
